analysis.one_liner: Extended federal minimum wage and immigration law to the Northern Marianas and restricted "Made in USA" labeling.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal minimum wage and immigration law did not apply to the Northern Mariana Islands, a U.S. commonwealth. Factories there could pay workers as little as $3.05 an hour under single-employer contracts the bill defines as indentured servitude, while their products shipped out with "Made in USA" labels. This bill would phase the federal minimum wage in, apply U.S. immigration law and the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, bar the "Made in USA" label unless workers were paid federal wages under lawful conditions, tie duty-free U.S. market access to fair-labor and anti-fraud requirements, require prevailing wages on federally funded construction there, and order studies of labor rights abuses and immigration security gaps.
analysis.who_benefits: The thousands of guest workers and garment workers in the Northern Marianas earning $3.05 an hour under contracts where displeasing the employer meant removal from the islands; American workers competing against imports made at sub-federal wages; consumers, who would get a truthful "Made in USA" label; and long-term guest workers, who could apply for permanent residence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Northern Marianas garment and guest workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would apply the federal minimum wage to the Northern Marianas, rising from $3.05 per hour to $3.60 in 2007, $4.15 in 2008, and by up to $1.00 per year until it matched the federal minimum wage.

Products leaving the islands could not be labeled "Made in USA" unless every direct-labor worker was paid at least the federal wage, federal labor and safety laws were followed, and no workers were held under conditions of indentured servitude.

The bill defines indentured servitude to include any alien worker whose presence depends on a contract with a single employer who controls how long the worker can stay — the structure of the islands' guest-worker system.

The Immigration and Nationality Act would apply to the islands as if they were a state, replacing local immigration rules, and long-term authorized guest workers meeting conditions could apply to adjust to permanent residence at no fee.

The Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000 would apply in the commonwealth, and federal funds could not be used for local construction projects unless workers received at least the federal minimum wage with weekly payment and posted wage scales.

The bill would condition duty-free, quota-free entry of Northern Marianas goods on fair labor practices and certified anti-transshipment controls, with penalties for exporters who falsify country of origin.

analysis.who_pays: Northern Marianas garment factory owners and other businesses that relied on paying below the federal minimum wage and on single-employer guest-worker contracts would bear higher labor costs and lose duty-free access if they did not comply. The island economy would absorb the transition, cushioned by a multi-year wage phase-in and a federally funded job-training and diversification program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Northern Marianas garment makers and low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Raising the minimum wage toward the federal level could push garment production out of the islands faster than a small, one-industry economy could replace those jobs; the bill's own phased schedule through 2008 and beyond, plus a $500,000-a-year diversification and training program, acknowledges that transition risk.

Applying U.S. immigration law would end the commonwealth's own guest-worker program, which hotel, construction, and other local businesses relied on, though the bill gives existing guest workers up to two years of continued authorization and a path to permanent residence.
Even at full compliance, the bill keeps the commonwealth's minimum wage below the federal rate until 2009 or later, so the reform is gradual rather than immediate relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: higher wages and enforceable labor and immigration law for island workers, against the risk of job losses in an economy built on the old system. The multi-year phase-in and transition assistance make the design more balanced than an immediate mandate, but the gradual schedule also means workers would not reach the federal wage for years. The labeling and duty-free provisions give manufacturers a clear market reason to comply rather than simply exit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, neither ever took it up, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the bill on June 7, 2006, joined by 30 Democratic cosponsors including then-Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi.
The House referred it to the Resources Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee the same day.
The record shows no hearings, markups, committee votes, or floor action of any kind afterward.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with the bill still pending in committee, so it expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Northern Marianas garment manufacturers and other island employers who paid below-federal wages and ran single-employer guest-worker contracts kept their cost advantage, and the commonwealth government kept control of its own labor and immigration rules. American consumers continued to buy "Made in USA" goods made at $3.05 an hour.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Northern Marianas garment manufacturers and low-wage employers

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a leading House Democrat; the bill died in the committees of the Republican-controlled House without a vote, so no roll call exists to measure the split.

industries.note: These factories produced apparel for the U.S. market at a $3.05 minimum wage under guest-worker contracts, using "Made in USA" labels and duty-free access. The bill removes both advantages unless they pay federal wages and follow federal labor law.

industries.industry: Island businesses relying on guest-worker contracts (tourism, construction, services)
industries.note: Federalizing immigration law would end the commonwealth's own guest-worker system that let employers control a worker's right to stay, though the bill provides a transition period and a possible path to permanent residence for long-term workers.

industries.industry: American apparel brands importing from the Northern Marianas
industries.note: They lost a low-cost, quota-free, "Made in USA" supply source under the bill, which consumers paid for in the form of misleading labels.

industries.industry: Northern Marianas construction contractors on federally funded projects
industries.note: Federal money could no longer go to local public works unless contractors paid at least the federal minimum wage with weekly payment and posted wage rates.
